evidence.observation: The it.each case 'converts %s tool throws to error output' drives executeToolCall (called at line 167) with both a synchronous and an asynchronous tool that throw, then asserts result.isError === true (line 169) and that the thrown message becomes the in-band error text (line 170). This is the primitive-path acceptance contract: a failed external effect is normalized to a non-success error result rather than escaping or being recorded as a terminal success.

The case 'lets abort-first gate refusal escape without invoking the tool' makes the real effect gate refuse admission before the effect and asserts that executeToolCall throws AbortRequested (symbol imported at line 5, asserted at line 180) while the tool's execute is never called. A refused or failed effect therefore cannot be turned into a success.

executeToolCall admits the effect through gate.admit, wraps the external tool invocation in a try/catch, and converts any thrown error into createErrorToolResult(...) with isError: true (lines 149-153), while the finally block stops accepting late updates. This is the primitive enforcement that a failed effect becomes error output and never a success.

publishToolIntent commits the durable retryable intent: it builds an effect_pending call carrying its replay policy (lines 200-205) and writes the resolved arguments to pi.op.tool_args (line 208) inside one lane.continueOperation commit, before any external effect is admitted. This effect_pending record is exactly the intent a crash can recover and retry.

startToolInvocation enforces intent-before-effect ordering: it awaits publishToolIntent (line 489) and only afterwards runs performToolInvocation (line 503) to execute the effect; a cancelled intent instead yields an aborted outcome (line 502). The effect can never run or complete without its durable intent already recorded.

recoverToolInvocation handles a persisted effect_pending call after restart: when both the call and the tool are replay-safe it re-executes the effect (retry, line 527-535), otherwise it reads the progress checkpoint and publishes interruptedOutcome (line 536-539), whose message ends with the INTERRUPTION_MARKER text 'external outcome is unknown'. A recovered effect is thus replayable or explicitly unknown, never a terminal success.

publishToolOutcome is the only transition that stages a tool result: it writes the tool-result message into the pending entry and moves the call to outcome_ready (lines 246-251). Because it runs strictly after executeToolCall, a failed effect surfaces here as an error message (isError true) rather than as a success.

ObservedMemoryStorage is the durable-commit witness: it records 'intent_commit' when pi.op.tool_args is written (line 80) and 'outcome_commit' when a pending entry is staged (line 85). The ordering test at lines 363-372 asserts intent_commit precedes tool_start, tool_update and outcome_commit, proving no outcome (and no success) can be staged before the retryable intent exists.

The case 'safe-replays persisted arguments and memos while interrupting unsafe effects' seeds two effect_pending calls and asserts the replay-safe one re-executes with its persisted arguments (lines 454-455) while the never-replay one is never executed (line 456) and is staged as isError with the 'external outcome is unknown' marker (lines 465-475). This is the durable-path acceptance of the failed-effect contract.

claims.claim: A tool effect that throws synchronously or asynchronously is normalized by executeToolCall into in-band error output (isError: true) instead of a successful result.
When the effect gate refuses admission before the effect, executeToolCall throws AbortRequested and the tool's execute is never invoked, so a refused effect cannot become a terminal success.
In the durable drive path the retryable effect_pending intent, including its replay policy and persisted arguments, is committed before the external effect is admitted.
Recovering a persisted effect_pending call either safely replays the effect or records an error with an unknown external outcome; it never converts the interrupted effect into a terminal success.

The durable layer cannot stage a tool result before the intent is committed: drive-tools.test.ts observes intent_commit strictly before tool_start and outcome_commit, and a cancelled effect stages a non-terminating isError result.

conclusion: The durable tool execution path satisfies the transferred contract: for every tool effect it first commits a durable, retryable effect_pending intent (with a replay policy and persisted arguments) and only then admits the external effect. A failing effect (sync throw, async throw, or gate refusal) is normalized to in-band error output with isError: true and is never recorded as a success; a persisted effect left effect_pending across a restart is either safely replayed or recorded as an error with an unknown external outcome. The required acceptance file packages/agent/test/harness/execution-tools.test.ts anchors this at the primitive layer (executeToolCall converts throws to error output; abort-first refusal throws AbortRequested without invoking the tool), and the drive-path source plus drive-tools.test.ts anchor the intent-before-effect ordering and the retry-or-unknown recovery semantics. The executable demo .prale-eval/contract-demo.mjs drives the real effect gate at runtime and statically asserts the remaining invariants; all 9 checks pass.

validation.notes: The executable contract demo ran with 9/9 checks passing (exit 0). It (a) behaviorally drives the real dependency-free effect gate from packages/agent/src/harness/execution/effect-gate.ts, confirming an admitted effect runs while abort-first and closed gates refuse admission with AbortRequested/terminal error and never invoke the effect, and (b) statically asserts the ordering and outcome invariants in packages/agent/src/harness/runtime/drive/tools.ts and packages/agent/src/harness/execution/tools.ts against the cited lines.
